title: Budgeting
description: Give every dollar a job. Learn the 50/30/20 rule and build your own budget.

lessons.title: What a budget is (and isn't)
body: A budget is a plan for your money. You decide ahead of time where each dollar goes.
A budget is not a punishment. It's how you make sure money goes to the things you care about most, instead of disappearing.
The simple formula: Income − Spending − Saving = What's left. If "what's left" is below zero, the plan needs to change.
lessons.keyIdea: A budget tells your money where to go, instead of wondering where it went.
lessons.example: You take home $600 a month. You plan $200 for needs, $150 for fun, $200 for savings, and keep $50 as a cushion.

lessons.title: The 50/30/20 rule
body: The 50/30/20 rule is an easy starting point for splitting take-home pay:

50% Needs: rent, groceries, phone, insurance, gas, minimum debt payments.
30% Wants: eating out, games, clothes beyond basics, hobbies.
20% Savings: emergency fund, goals, and extra debt payments.

It's a guide, not a rule. The warnings in the Budget Builder are guides too. If you live at home and have few bills, you can save way more than 20%. If rent is high, needs may go over 50% for a while.
lessons.keyIdea: Needs 50%, Wants 30%, Savings 20% of your take-home pay: a starting guide, not a rule.
lessons.example: Take-home pay of $2,000 → $1,000 needs, $600 wants, $400 savings.

lessons.title: Fixed vs. variable expenses
body: Fixed expenses are the same every month: rent, a phone plan, a streaming subscription, a car payment.
Variable expenses change month to month: groceries, gas, eating out, gifts.
Fixed costs are easy to plan. Variable costs are where budgets usually break, so track them closely for the first few months.
lessons.keyIdea: Cut variable expenses first. They're the easiest to change quickly.
lessons.example: Your $45 phone bill is fixed. Your food-with-friends spending ($30 one month, $90 the next) is variable.

lessons.title: Pay yourself first
body: Pay yourself first means you move money to savings the day you get paid, before you spend anything.
If you wait to save "whatever is left," there's usually nothing left.
Most banks let you set up an automatic transfer from checking to savings on payday. Set it once and forget it.
lessons.keyIdea: Savings is a bill you pay to your future self, first.
lessons.example: Every payday, $40 moves to savings automatically. You budget the rest and never miss it.

lessons.title: Track it and adjust
body: A budget is a guess. Tracking tells you what really happened.
Once a week, look at what you spent. Compare it to your plan. Over in one category? Take it from another category, not from savings.
Expect your first few budgets to be wrong. Every month you'll get closer. That's how everyone learns.
lessons.keyIdea: Plan → Track → Compare → Adjust. Repeat every month.
lessons.example: You planned $60 for eating out but spent $95. Next month you either plan $95 and cut clothes by $35, or eat out less.

lessons.title: Your monthly budget sheet
body: The Budget Builder is for planning. The Budget Sheet is for real life: one sheet for each month, filled in by you.
Each line has a Planned amount (your guess at the start of the month) and an Actual amount (what really happened). The Difference is Actual minus Planned.
Use the spending log to write down each purchase as it happens. At the end of the month, look at what went over, then copy the plan to next month and adjust.
lessons.keyIdea: Plan at the start of the month, track during it, compare at the end. Then copy and adjust.
lessons.example: You planned $50 for gas and spent $65. The sheet says “You spent $15.00 more than planned on Gas.” Next month you plan $65, and take the $15 from eating out.

samples.name: Teen with a part-time job
samples.note: Lives at home. Pays for own phone, gas, and fun. Saving for college and a car.

samples.name: First apartment

practice.prompt: Using the 50/30/20 rule, how much of a $2,000 take-home pay goes to needs?
Using 50/30/20, how much of $1,500 goes to wants?
Using 50/30/20, how much of $800 goes to savings?

practice.explanation: Groceries change every month. The others cost the same each month, so they are fixed.

practice.prompt: You take home $650. You planned $280 for needs, $190 for wants, and $120 for savings. How much is left over?
practice.explanation: $650 − $280 − $190 − $120 = $60 left. You could add it to savings or keep it as a cushion.

practice.prompt: You went $30 over on eating out this month. What's the best fix?
choices: Take $30 out of your emergency fund
Cut $30 from another want, like clothes or games
Stop budgeting since it didn't work
practice.explanation: Move money between categories, not out of savings. Budgets are supposed to be adjusted.
practice.reviewed: Judgment question; $30 appears in several choices on purpose.

quiz.prompt: In the 50/30/20 rule, what does the 20 stand for?
quiz.explanation: 20% goes to savings, which includes paying extra on debt.

quiz.prompt: Your take-home pay is $3,000 a month. Using 50/30/20, how much is for needs?
Should you build your budget on gross pay or net pay?
choices: Net pay, it's what you actually get
quiz.explanation: Budget with net (take-home) pay. Taxes are already gone before you can spend it.

choices: Move money into savings as soon as you're paid
quiz.explanation: Save first, then spend what's left, instead of saving what's left after spending.

quiz.prompt: You take home $1,800. Using 50/30/20, how much goes to savings?

quiz.explanation: Rent is the same every month. The others change, so they're variable.

quiz.prompt: Income: $900. Spending: rent share $300, phone $50, food $200, fun $150, savings $150. How much is left?
Your needs take up 60% of your pay because rent is high. What's a smart move?
choices: Shrink wants for now so savings stays healthy, and look for ways to lower needs
Put the extra on a credit card
quiz.explanation: 50/30/20 is a guide. When needs run high, trim wants first and keep saving something.

flashcards.back: A plan for where every dollar of your income goes.
50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings (of take-home pay). A guide, not a rule.
A cost that's the same each month, like rent or a phone plan.
A cost that changes each month, like groceries or gas.
Move money to savings right when you're paid, before spending.
Spending more than you planned (or more than you earn). Fix it by adjusting other categories.
